level.name: Advanced
level.description: Develop precise, flexible English for complex academic, professional, and abstract communication, with emphasis on nuance, inference, cohesion, and register.

topics.title: Inversion for Emphasis
topics.objective: Use inversion after negative and restrictive adverbials to create formal or emphatic structures.
topics.theory: After negative or restrictive adverbials such as never, rarely, seldom, hardly, no sooner, only then, and not until, auxiliary-subject inversion is often required. This structure is especially common in formal written English and emphatic speech.
examples: Never have I seen such a rapid change.
Rarely do we receive complaints of this kind.
Not until the meeting ended did she explain the problem.
No sooner had we arrived than the system failed.

common_mistakes.wrong: Never I have seen this.
common_mistakes.correct: Never have I seen this.

common_mistakes.wrong: Not until Friday she replied.
common_mistakes.correct: Not until Friday did she reply.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct inversion.
Rarely ___ such a detailed response.
Not until the report was published ___ the scale of the issue.
questions.explanation: Not until triggers inversion in the main clause.

questions.prompt: No sooner ___ the announcement than the website crashed.
questions.explanation: No sooner commonly takes past perfect inversion.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_a: Only then we realized the risk.
questions.option_b: Only then did we realize the risk.
questions.option_c: Only then we did realized the risk.
questions.option_d: Only then realized we the risk always.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Under no circumstances should confidential files be shared externally.' What does the structure emphasize?
Which sentence contains an error?

questions.option_b: Not until noon did they respond.
questions.option_d: Never we have experienced this delay.

questions.prompt: Hardly ___ the meeting when another issue emerged.
What does the speaker emphasize?
questions.option_b: The speed of the change was exceptional
questions.explanation: The inversion stresses how unusual the change was.
questions.audio_text: Never have I seen a department adapt so quickly to a new operating model.

questions.prompt: When did the team understand the consequences?
questions.option_b: Only after the data were reviewed
questions.audio_text: Only after we reviewed the full dataset did we understand the consequences of the change.

passages.title: A Sudden Policy Shift
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What caused leadership to reconsider?
What did the survey suggest?
Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_a: Rarely had employees reacted so strongly.
questions.option_b: Only after the survey did leadership reconsider.
questions.option_c: Never before had the company received so much feedback.
questions.option_d: Not only employees questioned the plan, but managers warned too.
questions.explanation: The emphatic structure requires inversion: 'Not only did employees question...'.

passages.content_text: Rarely had employees reacted so strongly to an internal policy change. The company had announced that all staff would be expected to return to the office five days a week, despite having operated successfully under a hybrid model for nearly three years. Not only did employees question the practical reasons for the decision, but several managers also warned that retention could become a problem. Only after the human-resources team presented survey data did senior leadership reconsider the plan. The data showed that a significant number of experienced employees were actively exploring other jobs. Never before had the company received so much internal feedback in such a short period. Within two weeks, the original proposal was replaced by a more flexible arrangement. Under no circumstances, management later admitted, should such a major change have been introduced without consultation.

topics.title: Cleft Sentences and Emphatic Structures
topics.objective: Use cleft and pseudo-cleft sentences to highlight specific information.
topics.theory: Cleft structures divide information so that one element receives special focus. Common patterns include 'It was X that...', 'What I need is...', and 'The reason why... is...'.
examples: It was the timing that caused the problem.
What we need is a clearer strategy.
The reason why I left was the lack of support.
What surprised me most was the speed of the response.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was because the cost why we canceled.
common_mistakes.correct: It was the cost that caused us to cancel.

common_mistakes.wrong: What I need are a solution.
common_mistakes.correct: What I need is a solution.

questions.option_a: It was the deadline that caused concern.
questions.option_b: It the deadline was caused concern.
questions.option_c: Was the deadline that concern caused.
questions.option_d: It was caused concern the deadline.

questions.prompt: Complete: What we need ___ a more realistic timeline.

questions.option_b: It was the budget that caused the delay.

Which sentence contains an error?

questions.option_c: The reason why we left was the noise.
questions.option_d: What I need are a clear explanation.

passages.title: Why the Project Failed
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What did the review identify as the main weakness?
questions.explanation: Unclear ownership was the key weakness.

questions.prompt: What made the situation worse?
Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_a: What caused delays was unclear ownership.
questions.option_b: It was not software complexity that mattered most.
questions.option_c: The reason why deadlines were missed was the lack of process.
questions.option_d: What the company learned were that governance mattered.
questions.explanation: Use 'What the company learned was that...'.

passages.content_text: When the project was reviewed, several explanations were suggested. Some managers blamed the technology, while others pointed to limited staffing. However, what the independent review identified as the main weakness was unclear ownership. It was not the complexity of the software that caused the greatest delays; it was the fact that no single team had responsibility for final decisions. What made the situation worse was that departments were using different approval procedures. The reason why several deadlines were missed was not a lack of effort but the absence of a shared process. Once those findings were accepted, management created a single governance structure. What the company learned from the experience was that technical problems are often easier to solve than organizational ones.

topics.title: Advanced Modal Meaning
topics.objective: Interpret and use subtle modal meanings involving criticism, expectation, probability, and unrealized possibility.
topics.theory: Advanced modal patterns include should have, needn't have, could have, might have, ought to have, and was/were supposed to. Meaning depends on whether an action happened and how the speaker evaluates it.
examples: You should have told me earlier.
We needn't have booked so many rooms.
She could have won.
They were supposed to arrive at six.
He might well have misunderstood.

common_mistakes.wrong: We didn't need to book, so we booked unnecessarily = needn't have booked.
common_mistakes.correct: Use 'needn't have booked' when the action happened but was unnecessary.

common_mistakes.wrong: She should have went.
common_mistakes.correct: She should have gone.

questions.prompt: You ___ me earlier; I could have helped.
questions.explanation: Should have expresses criticism about a past action.

questions.prompt: We ___ so much food; half of it was left.
questions.explanation: The purchase happened but was unnecessary.

questions.prompt: She ___ the competition, but she made one mistake at the end.
questions.explanation: Could have expresses unrealized past possibility.

questions.prompt: They were ___ to send the contract yesterday.
He ___ misunderstood the instructions; the wording was ambiguous.
questions.explanation: Might well have expresses a fairly plausible possibility.

questions.prompt: Read: 'We needn't have hired an extra room because only ten people attended.' What is implied?
questions.explanation: Needn't have means the action happened but was unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_d: He ought to have went earlier.

questions.prompt: The delivery was ___ to arrive by noon, but it didn't.
What does the speaker criticize?
questions.audio_text: We should have checked the figures before sending the report to the client.

passages.title: A Preventable Error
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What should the analyst have done?
questions.option_a: Checked the source table more carefully
questions.explanation: The text explicitly criticizes the checking process.

questions.prompt: Why was the rush unnecessary?
Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_a: The manager could have requested a review.
questions.option_c: The error might have been avoided.
questions.option_d: The analyst should have checkeded the table.

passages.content_text: After a financial report was sent to a client, the team discovered that two figures had been copied incorrectly. The mistake did not affect the overall conclusion, but it created unnecessary confusion. The analyst who prepared the report should have checked the source table more carefully. The manager admitted that she could have asked a second person to review the document before it was sent. In fact, the team needn't have rushed the report because the client later confirmed that the deadline had been flexible. Several colleagues argued that the error might well have been avoided if the normal review process had been followed. The department has now introduced a rule requiring two people to check high-value reports.

topics.title: Advanced and Inverted Conditionals
topics.objective: Use formal conditional inversion and nuanced alternatives to standard if-clauses.
topics.theory: In formal English, conditional clauses can be inverted by removing 'if': 'Had I known...', 'Were I to...', 'Should you need...'. These structures are common in formal writing and hypothetical discussion.
examples: Had I known, I would have acted differently.
Were the situation to change, we would review the policy.
Should you require assistance, contact reception.
Had it not been for the delay, we would have finished.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had I knew, I would have called.
common_mistakes.correct: Had I known, I would have called.

common_mistakes.wrong: Should you will need help, call us.
common_mistakes.correct: Should you need help, call us.

questions.prompt: Choose the formal equivalent of 'If I had known'.
questions.explanation: Past perfect conditional inversion uses Had + subject + participle.

questions.prompt: ___ you require further information, please contact us.
questions.explanation: Should + subject + base verb is a formal conditional.

questions.prompt: ___ the market to decline further, we would revise the forecast.
questions.explanation: Were + subject + to-infinitive expresses a formal hypothetical.

questions.explanation: This is an inverted third conditional.

questions.option_b: Were I accept the role, I relocate.
questions.option_c: Should I would accept, I relocate.

questions.option_b: Should you need help, call me.

passages.title: A Contingency Plan
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What will happen if severe weather affects transport?
questions.explanation: The app will be used for notifications.

Which sentence is incorrect?

questions.option_b: Were the venue unavailable, sessions would move.
questions.option_c: Had arrangements not existed, events might have been canceled.
questions.option_d: Should weather will worsen, participants will be notified.

passages.content_text: The organization has prepared a detailed contingency plan for the upcoming conference. Should severe weather affect transport, participants will be notified through the event app. Were the main venue to become unavailable, sessions would be moved to a nearby university building. Had such arrangements not been made in previous years, several events would have been canceled. The organizers have also agreed that, should attendance exceed expectations, additional rooms will be opened. Were it not for these backup arrangements, the event would be far more vulnerable to disruption. The plan is deliberately cautious because the conference attracts visitors from several countries and even a minor transport problem can affect hundreds of participants.

topics.title: Participle Clauses
topics.objective: Use present, past, and perfect participle clauses to express time, reason, result, and background efficiently.
topics.theory: Participle clauses can make advanced writing more concise. Present participles often show simultaneous or resulting actions; past participles often have passive meaning; perfect participles show earlier completed actions.
examples: Having finished the report, she sent it to the client.
Built in the 19th century, the house requires restoration.
Working from home, he saved two hours a day.
Not knowing the answer, I stayed silent.

common_mistakes.wrong: Having finished the report, the email was sent by Marta.
common_mistakes.correct: Having finished the report, Marta sent the email.

common_mistakes.wrong: Built in 1920, they renovated the house.
common_mistakes.correct: Built in 1920, the house was later renovated.

questions.prompt: ___ the report, she emailed the client.
questions.explanation: Perfect participle shows the report was completed first.

questions.prompt: ___ in 1890, the building is protected.
Choose the sentence with correct subject reference.

questions.option_b: Driving to work, I heard the news.
questions.option_c: Having finished, the computer was shut down by me.
questions.option_d: Built in 1920, they renovated the house.

passages.title: Restoring a Landmark
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Why does the hall require restoration?
questions.explanation: Decades of heavy use caused deterioration.

questions.prompt: What did engineers discover after examining the roof?
Which sentence is incorrect?

questions.option_b: Having examined the roof, engineers found damage.
questions.option_c: Not wanting to close the building, the team chose phases.
questions.option_d: Having finished the phase, the entrance was reopened by nobody specified.

passages.content_text: Built more than a century ago, the Central Hall has become one of the city's most recognizable buildings. Having suffered decades of heavy use, however, it now requires extensive restoration. Working with conservation specialists, the city has developed a plan that aims to preserve the original structure while improving accessibility and energy efficiency. Having examined the roof, engineers discovered several areas of serious water damage. Designed before modern safety standards existed, some staircases will also need modification. Not wanting to close the building completely, the project team plans to carry out the work in stages. Having completed the first phase, they will reopen the main entrance before beginning work on the eastern wing.

topics.title: Hedging and Cautious Language
topics.objective: Express claims, interpretations, and recommendations with appropriate degrees of certainty.
topics.theory: Academic and professional English often avoids absolute claims. Hedging devices include may, might, appears to, seems to, tends to, is likely to, suggests, arguably, relatively, and to some extent.
examples: The results suggest that the policy may be effective.
The change appears to have reduced delays.
This approach is likely to be more sustainable.
The evidence is relatively limited.

common_mistakes.wrong: The data prove that this always works.
common_mistakes.correct: The data suggest that this may work.

common_mistakes.wrong: This definitely causes every problem.
common_mistakes.correct: This may contribute to the problem.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is most appropriately hedged?
questions.option_a: This policy definitely solves the problem.
questions.option_b: The findings suggest that the policy may help.

questions.prompt: Which phrase expresses cautious interpretation?
questions.explanation: Appears to is a standard hedge.

questions.prompt: The results ___ indicate a modest improvement.
Which phrase means 'partly'?
questions.explanation: To some extent limits the claim.

questions.prompt: Which is most suitable in an academic discussion?
questions.option_a: Arguably, the policy created unintended effects.

questions.prompt: Read: 'The evidence is relatively limited.' What does 'relatively' do?
Which statement is least appropriately hedged?
questions.option_a: The findings may indicate a trend.
questions.option_b: The change appears to have helped.
questions.option_d: The results prove this is always true.
questions.explanation: The last claim is overly absolute.

questions.prompt: This factor is ___ to have influenced the outcome.
questions.explanation: Be likely to is a standard hedging pattern.

questions.prompt: How certain is the speaker?
questions.audio_text: The early results appear to be positive, although the sample is still relatively small.

passages.title: Interpreting Research Results
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Why should the findings not be generalized too broadly?
questions.option_a: All participants came from one industry

questions.prompt: What is the study's cautious conclusion?
questions.option_b: It may help under certain conditions
questions.explanation: The authors avoid a universal claim.

questions.prompt: Which version is least cautious?
questions.option_c: is unlikely to produce the same result everywhere
questions.option_d: proves flexible work is always superior
questions.explanation: The final claim is absolute and unsupported.

passages.content_text: A recent study examined whether flexible working arrangements influence employee productivity. The researchers reported a small average increase in completed tasks among employees who worked remotely two days a week. However, the authors emphasized that the effect was not consistent across all roles. The findings suggest that flexible work may be beneficial for tasks requiring long periods of concentration, whereas highly collaborative roles may gain less. It is also possible that some of the reported improvement resulted from employees changing how they recorded their work. The sample was relatively large, but all participants came from the same industry. Consequently, the findings cannot necessarily be generalized to every workplace. Overall, the study appears to support a cautious conclusion: flexibility may improve productivity under certain conditions, but it is unlikely to produce the same result in every organization.

topics.title: Nominalisation and Formal Style
topics.objective: Transform clauses into noun-based structures to create concise, formal academic and professional writing.
topics.theory: Nominalisation turns verbs or adjectives into nouns, often making writing denser and more formal. For example, 'The company decided to expand' can become 'The company's decision to expand'. Excessive nominalisation can make text difficult, so use it selectively.
examples: The committee decided to postpone the vote. → The committee's decision to postpone the vote...
Prices increased rapidly. → The rapid increase in prices...
The system failed because maintenance was inadequate. → The failure resulted from inadequate maintenance.

common_mistakes.wrong: The decide of the committee...
common_mistakes.correct: The committee's decision...

common_mistakes.wrong: The improve of efficiency...
common_mistakes.correct: The improvement in efficiency...

Noun form of 'implement':
Choose the more formal nominalised version.

questions.option_c: The company did reduce costs a lot.
questions.explanation: The noun phrase creates a formal style.

passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

What delayed adoption?
questions.explanation: The text states insufficient training delayed adoption.

passages.content_text: The implementation of the new procurement system was followed by a noticeable reduction in processing time. Before the change, the approval of routine purchases often required several manual checks. The introduction of automated validation reduced duplication and improved consistency. However, the initial configuration of the system created difficulties for some departments. A lack of clear documentation contributed to confusion, while insufficient training delayed adoption. Following an internal review, management approved the development of new guidance materials and the expansion of user training. The subsequent improvement in staff confidence was reflected in fewer support requests. Although the system still requires refinement, the overall assessment has been positive.

topics.title: Advanced Passive Reporting Structures
topics.objective: Use impersonal and personal passive reporting structures in formal communication.
topics.theory: Formal reporting often uses structures such as 'It is believed that...', 'The company is expected to...', and 'He is thought to have...'. Perfect infinitives can report earlier actions.
examples: It is believed that demand will rise.

The suspect is thought to have left the country.
The policy is reported to have reduced costs.

common_mistakes.correct: The company is expected to announce results.

common_mistakes.wrong: He is thought to left.
common_mistakes.correct: He is thought to have left.

questions.explanation: Perfect infinitive reports an earlier action.

passages.content_text: Interest rates are expected to remain stable over the next quarter, although some analysts believe a small reduction is possible later in the year. Inflation is reported to have fallen more quickly than originally predicted, while consumer confidence is thought to be recovering gradually. The central bank is understood to be monitoring wage growth particularly closely. Several economists are said to have revised their forecasts after the latest employment figures were published. The economy is not expected to return to rapid growth immediately, but conditions are generally believed to be improving.

topics.title: Advanced Relative Clauses and Substitution
topics.objective: Use complex relative structures and substitution to avoid repetition and improve cohesion.
topics.theory: Advanced relative structures include preposition + whom/which, quantifier + whom/which, and reduced repetition through one/ones, so, do so, and that of/those of.
examples: The report on which the decision was based...
Several participants, many of whom were experts,...
The first proposal was stronger than the second one.
Some teams adopted the policy; others chose not to do so.
The results differ from those of last year.

passages.content_text: The committee reviewed two proposals, both of which met the technical requirements. passages.content_text: The recently announced regional rail expansion program is one of the largest infrastructure projects proposed in the area for decades. The long-term economic impact of improved connections between smaller towns and the capital is expected to be significant. However, the projected construction cost of the first phase has already attracted criticism. Residents living near the planned route have raised concerns about noise, land acquisition, and the potential loss of green space. The independent environmental assessment commissioned by the transport authority is due to be published next month. passages.content_text: The negotiations had reached a critical stage. Both sides had raised concerns about cost, and neither wanted to take responsibility for additional risk. At first, there appeared to be little room for compromise. However, after several hours of discussion, the teams began to identify areas where they could adjust their positions. The supplier agreed to meet the original delivery deadline, while the client accepted a phased payment schedule. On balance, both sides felt the agreement was preferable to starting again with a new partner. One legal issue remained a grey area, but the teams decided it did not pose an immediate threat to implementation. By the end of the meeting, they had reached a compromise and were able to move forward.

passages.content_text: During a project review, a senior manager presented an ambitious plan to launch a new service within six weeks. The technical lead responded, 'It's an interesting target, although we may want to look carefully at the testing schedule.' A finance manager added, 'I wonder whether the current budget gives us enough flexibility.' Neither speaker directly said that the plan was unrealistic, but both were expressing reservations. Later, when the senior manager suggested reducing the testing period, the technical lead said, 'I'm not sure that would be advisable.' The discussion remained polite, but the implied message was clear: the team believed the launch date involved significant risk.

passages.title: Should Public Data Be Open by Default?
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What is the main counterargument?
questions.option_a: Open data may create privacy and security risks
questions.explanation: Risk is the principal opposing concern.

questions.prompt: How does the writer respond?
questions.option_a: By proposing a risk-based balanced approach
questions.option_c: By demanding all data remain closed

questions.option_d: Open data always produces huge benefits everywhere.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly qualifies the scale of benefits.

passages.content_text: Supporters of open public data argue that making government datasets easier to access can improve transparency and encourage innovation. Researchers, journalists, and businesses may all benefit from information that would otherwise remain difficult to obtain. Critics, however, point out that publication can create privacy and security risks, particularly when datasets contain detailed geographic or personal information. This objection is important, but it does not necessarily justify keeping all data closed. A more balanced approach would distinguish between information that can be released safely and information that requires aggregation, anonymization, or restricted access. Evidence from existing open-data programs suggests that public access can generate social and economic value, although the scale of those benefits varies. Therefore, the strongest argument is not that all public data should be open without restriction, but that openness should be the starting principle where risks can be managed responsibly.

passages.content_text: The company described the launch of its new customer platform as a major success. Technically, the system went live on schedule, and more than eighty percent of existing customers activated their accounts during the first week. The experience was not entirely smooth, however. Support requests tripled, several users reported difficulty accessing older records, and one payment function was temporarily disabled. Management emphasized the high activation rate in its public statement, while internal teams focused more heavily on the unresolved technical issues. The platform may ultimately prove successful, but the first week provides a useful reminder that launch dates and adoption figures do not tell the whole story. Calling the rollout a complete success at this stage would be, at best, premature.

passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What did both studies agree on?

passages.content_text: A public agency commissioned two independent studies before deciding whether to replace its existing case-management system. The first study focused on technical performance and concluded that the current platform was becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. It recommended replacement within two years. The second study examined user experience and found that staff were dissatisfied with several features but were concerned about the disruption associated with a major transition. Although the studies emphasized different issues, both agreed that doing nothing would create growing costs. Taken together, the findings suggest that replacement is justified, but that implementation should be gradual. A phased approach would allow technical problems to be addressed while giving staff time to adapt. For senior management, the key decision is therefore not whether change is needed, but how quickly it should occur and how much support users will require.

passages.audio_text: Taken together, the technical and financial reviews support proceeding with the project, although both identify implementation risks. In practical terms, this means approval should be accompanied by a phased rollout and formal review points.
